utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Albiston, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, just before we ended for the day, I was asking you some questions about the practice of not investigating killings after Operation Storm, and yesterday you agreed that the killings that were taking place were one of the most serious and immediate problems of crime in the aftermath of Operation Storm, and, therefore, that it should have been a focus of police resources. And then I asked you if the practice of not investigating killings was inconsistent with your view of what the policing priority should have been, and you mentioned certain post-conflict obstacles, such as a lack of territorial control. And then I asked you about whether -- if a sanitation team could collect bodies, whether that indicated an investigation could take place. And I'd like to hopefully clear this up by asking this in a more concrete way by reference to an example that you're aware of, which is Grubori. And you stated yesterday that you were aware that there was no investigation into the killings in Grubori and that the bodies were sanitised, and that was at page 91. Now, in relation to that incident, there was no obstacle to investigating those killings relating to the post-conflict situation, was there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly aware of no obstacle from the position of civilian policing, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So that was an example where the Croatian authorities could have investigated, but did not, based on your review and assessment of the evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar as I can see, I can see no reason why.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you a question about whether, in reviewing the material you were provided, whether you saw evidence of an attitude of tolerance or indifference on the part of the Croatian authorities towards the crimes of looting and burning and killing, and I'd just like to review a few examples so that you know what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, the previous answer of the witness was: "Insofar as I can see, I can see no reason why." The question was that it was an example that they could have investigated, but they did not. Now, it's not entirely clear, but I understood your answer to be that you did not see any reason why they had not investigated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the first example is from an HRAT report for the 12th of August, and this is P32, and it refers to a meeting with General Cermak, and the report states that: "In a meeting with the sector commander, Cermak stated that life in Knin and in the sector was getting back to normal. He responded to an inquiry for information concerning the rash of fires throughout the area by insisting that the phenomenon had no official sanction and that action is being taken by authorities to stop it." It's at the bottom of this page: "The position appears to be belied by the substantial number of HV military personnel and Croatian civilian police, who are observed passing areas of major conflagration without stopping or, indeed, appearing to take notice of the ongoing destruction." Another example is the evidence of Mr. Jan Elleby, who was the deputy chief then chief of UN CIVPOL in Sector South, and he stated that some attempts were made to stop the looting, but in his view, it was not very persistent, nor did the police seem interested. And he recalled an example of observing a soldier carrying a stereo out of a building and walking past a police officer, who did nothing. That's at P215, page 3. Another example is an ECMM report for the 4th of September, describing the killing of an old lady in the village of Palaca. The report notes that the ECMM team had found a lot of blood and one bullet shell in the house of the killed lady, and the answer of Croatian police concerning this case was that the old woman died because she had low blood pressure. And that's at P2157, paragraph 4. And an ECC monitor named Mr. Eric Hendriks gave evidence of what he described as an unwillingness on the part of the authorities to stop the criminal acts, and he based this, in part, on his observation that he saw policemen hanging around the center of Knin or manning check-points with five to seven men, just stopping the cars of international organisations, while trucks and civilian cars would pass without being checked. And that's at D820, page 3. And the last example is a UN CIVPOL weekly report for the 21st to 26th of August, and the report states on page 5 that: "On the 23rd of August, at a meeting with the chief of police for Drnis, UN CIVPOL learned that no one had been booked for arson up until that point, and the chief of police stated that, in his opinion, most of the houses were burning because of electrical faults." And that's at P230, page 5. Now, my question is: Did you see evidence like this, and do you agree that it's evidence of an attitude of tolerance or indifference towards crimes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an awful lot in the question, and I certainly do not intend to try to address and dismiss each of the things that you've raised, because when I read the documents, I saw the examples and others of the sort which you have mentioned, and taken as a whole, they present a very unsatisfactory picture of police efforts and, indeed, efforts of many people. I think there are other factors to take into consideration, and I don't say what I'm about to say by way of excusing bad behaviour by individuals. Policemen, in my experience, are not very good at putting out fires. Policemen, when told to stand on check-points and check vehicles, are reluctant to undertake other duties which might result in them failing to discharge the duties to which they have been allocated. There are, as I suggested yesterday, many things which make civilian policing in these sorts of conditions problematic. I don't, for one moment, try to excuse or dismiss the sort of problems to which you alluded in your question. I think that it is extremely likely, on my reading of the evidence, that some of the civilian policemen who were engaged in this area at this time had a problem with attitude. Maybe that's an expression which we use in our job which doesn't translate particularly well, but let me put it this way: Their attitude towards the efficient discharge of their duties may not always be what it should be, and their attitude towards the impartial discharge of their duties may not always be what it ought to be. Those problems exist in policing worldwide, and they come to the fore in periods of violence and, particularly, inter-communal or ethnic or religious violence. I think that's fairly well known, and I don't doubt that there were instances of it here. And the sort of examples which you cite in your question may well be that. If we look at whether that was organised or tolerated, well, I think you would have to examine the conduct of individual supervising officers. In this case, in the lower ranks, some of the supervising officers may not have been performing their duties particularly well if the policemen under their command were not performing their duties very well. But so far as the documents relating to policy are concerned, I think they show a rather different story, and we went over that ground yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's quite a bit in that answer. I'd just like to pick up on one thing you is said, which is: "I think it's extremely likely, on my reading of the evidence, that the civilian policemen who were engaged in this area at this time had a problem with attitude." Now, based on your review of the evidence, did you consider this likelihood of a problem with attitude to be something that may have affected the performance of the Croatian authorities in addressing crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I think the problems to which you have alluded, they're not generic, or from my reading of the documents they are not -- they don't permeate the entire civilian police. There are examples of poor policing, which I would expect to find, and I make no attempt to excuse that. In fact, quite the contrary. From my professional perspective, of course, I take a very dim view of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, for example, when the HRAT report states that the position of General Cermak that action is being taken by authorities to stop the crimes is belied by the substantial number of HV and civilian police who are observed passing areas of major conflagration without stopping or, indeed, appearing to take notice of the ongoing destruction, that's not something that, in your view, would permeate the entire civilian police or the entire system at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that observation by that witness carries all the implications which I feel that are conveyed in your question, because the people concerned, who were identified passing by, may well have had other priorities that they were being directed to attend to. I don't know the answer to that on the basis of the document which you cite.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, when I read a number of examples to you, you confirmed that you had seen examples like that and --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- many more?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in light of the clear number of times you've seen similar observations, I'm wondering how you can conclude that that's not something that permeated the system at the time, if monitor after monitor is saying the same thing based on similar observations.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what monitor after monitor is seeing is significant disorder. They're seeing looting and burning, which they report, because that's what monitors do, that's what monitors are looking for. And I think in this circumstances, that's -- in these circumstances, that's what monitors are expecting to find. I don't think it necessarily follows that a failure of the police to address all these issues quickly and effectively can be attributed to the sort of reasons which I think you're suggesting. I think there are many more reasons which are also -- it's also necessary to bring into the equation, including shortage of resources, the need to perform other directed duties, the need to establish control over the situation, and so on. I think there's sometimes -- there's sometimes a danger, when people are making comments on these situations, that they don't appreciate the level of chaos, the difficulty with communications, with effective command and control, and so on, that all large organisations experience in their day-to-day work and especially in situations in which they're deployed operationally to deal with difficult problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Albiston. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, are you ready to re-examine the witness? In view of what I said yesterday as far as cross-examination is concerned, Ms. Higgins, do you consider it -- and I'm also addressing you, Mr. Kehoe. Do you consider it the proper sequence that you'll now re-examine or that first an opportunity would be given to Mr. Kehoe to address the matters he apparently had on his mind and which could be considered as a matter which is a matter being raised in cross-examination rather than in re-cross? I'm asking your view on what would be the proper order, and I'll give an opportunity to Mr. Kehoe as well to address that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In my submission, Your Honour, I have discussed with Mr. Kehoe the area of questioning that he wishes to undertake this morning, and given that they do not overlap, it would, in my submission, be appropriate for me to re-examine Mr. Albiston and then for Mr. Kehoe to address the issues he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to raise the matter, but, Mr. Kehoe, I take it that since Ms. Higgins is reporting on the result of your conversations, that you would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know yesterday we talked about cross, and I wanted to raise that issue, but we're done. I may have one or two questions in re-cross related to the testimony that was forthcoming from Ms. Gustafson's cross. So it may be covered by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- Ms. Higgins, it may not, just for Your Honours' knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- if Ms. Higgins has no problem, even not knowing what the areas are you'll cover --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We did discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you did discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, Ms. Higgins, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, I want to raise with you, first of all, a matter that was raised this morning. You were asked the question, in reviewing the material you were provided, whether you saw evidence of an attitude of tolerance or indifference on the part of the Croatian authorities towards the crimes of looting and burning and killing. And then Ms. Gustafson referred to a few examples which she put to you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, when you wrote your report, Mr. Albiston, you refer to what can only be described from paragraph 3.63 as a ream of documentation between Mr. Moric and Lausic, and also police administrations. And if you can go to that section of your report, what I intend to do, rather than pulling all these documents up, is to go through them briefly and to see if you recollect these documents, which might enable you to give a fuller answer to the question that was posed to you this morning. Are you with me, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The first document, for the record, is D50, which was a Moric order to police administrations in which he referred to asking to be informed about whether or not there was cooperation between the police administrations and the fact that he had ordered linking with the military police in order to stop houses being burnt and other people's movable property being taken away unlawfully in the liberated territory. And that date was the 22nd of August, 1995. You may also recall in that document that he asked whether or not on-site investigations were being carried out and whether or not crimes were being investigated. Do you recall the tenor of that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and others like it, in particular where Mr. Moric is lambasting his junior officers for the reports not being up to the standard or in the timeliness that he required.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Indeed. Now the next document, D49, again, just to put the tenor for your recollection, a document from Josko Moric, dated of the 18th of August, to police administrations, referring again to the torching of houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property, and he refers to: "In order to put a stop to this problem, I order, inter alia, on-site investigations, forensic and operative processing." And he goes on to state that: "If the military police cannot perform the task of investigation and forensic and operative processing, the civilian police will do it alone, irrespective of whether the perpetrator wears a Croatian Army uniform or not." Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Next document, D574, for the record, document from Josko Moric to the police administrations, which again refers to the fact that: "We requested a report on linkage with the military police in order to prevent further torching of houses and illegal taking of movable property," dated the 30th of August. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document that you cite, Mr. Albiston, is a document from Josko Moric again to the police administrations, dated the 11th of September, ordering the supply of joint data concerning the burning of houses, illegal appropriation of other people's movable property, cooperation with the military police, and implementing measures for the period between the 22nd of August and the 10th of September. Familiar?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Next document, D594, dated the 13th of September, another document from Josko Moric which again refers to this, the need for a joint operational meeting in order to assess the situation and problems, which included the level of public law and order and the level of protection of lives and property for all people. Familiar to you, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One more, D597, dated the 2nd of October, again from Josko Moric to the civilian police administrations: "Submit combined information for the period between the 22nd of August and the 2nd of October on murders, arsons, explosions, property seizure. Conducted on-site investigations. Perpetrators known. Unknown perpetrators, and abuse of uniform."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: A document you cite, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And then you also cite a collection of documents from within the civilian police authorities concerning reports back to Josko Moric, which include: D7 -- sorry, D573, dated the 24th of August, from Drago Matic; D575, another report back from Drago Matic, dated the 1st of September; D580, another report back, dated the 12th of September, Drago Matic again; and there are also references in your report, a number of them, concerning joint meetings to stop crime. Do you remember that collection of documents --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One more, D584: "More joint meetings in respect of law and order." That is just a mere flavour of the documents you cite in your report. Now, you have been asked that question, and Ms. Gustafson relied on three examples -- three or four examples that she cited to you. Please answer the question in the round, taking into account the evidence that you have cited in your report as to whether or not there was an attitude of tolerance or indifference on the part of Croatian authorities towards crime of looting, burning, and killing.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the short answer is, No. And I think to the list of documents, we might usefully add D595. What I was trying to convey in my answer to Ms. Gustafson was that whilst an examination or my examination of the documents did not reveal any high-level behaviour of the type which I think Ms. Gustafson is suggesting, it is nevertheless frequently the case, and appears to have been the case in these particular circumstances, that in times of significant violence and disorder, there will be failings in individual police operations and in the behaviour of individual police officers, and I don't think that that would be disputed on the basis of the evidence. That's not the same thing as saying that this behaviour or these failings were in any way tolerated by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, I heard a question put by Ms. Gustafson about evidence of an attitude of tolerance or indifference, not authorities. So you changed the question a bit. I look at page 5, lines 6 and 7, where Ms. Gustafson, at least in that instance, is not primarily referring to authorities. Therefore, in order to then later say, Well, you gave an answer to this question, where you put a different question to the witness, and of course it's perfectly clear that the examples given by Ms. Gustafson are reports of what was observed on the ground, and the witness explained to us what he expected monitors to look for. But you are citing, if I could say, a different type of evidence; that is, how the -- those on a higher level, responsible for the functioning of the police, what they put on paper. And, therefore, it's difficult for me to understand why you rephrase the question by Ms. Gustafson in the way you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, I refer you to page 3, where the question reads: "... whether you saw evidence of an attitude of tolerance or indifference on the part of the Croatian authorities towards the crimes of looting and burning and killing." I accept the examples that Ms. Gustafson has put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were all -- and then the question was again phrased without the authorities being mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, the two questions are there, Your Honour, on the record, and in my submission, I'm entitled to ask Mr. Albiston about the examples that he has cited. The question is broadly phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you referred to the second question because you were referring to the three examples only given by Ms. Gustafson. So I expect then that you would refer to the question that was at that moment put by Ms. Gustafson. But let's -- let's continue, and let's clearly keep in mind that apparently, from the questioning, it appears that two levels are addressed in the questions and in the documents as to indifference and tolerance.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. If we could just move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, you have been asked to distinguish clearly between three concepts, in fact. One is de facto command and control, one is de jure command and control, and the other which we've referred to is a concept of influence. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, at various places during the course of your testimony, leaving aside your report for the moment, you have stated that Mr. Cermak had no de facto command over the police. For the record, transcript pages 23948 to 9, and 23837 to 8; transcript 23992; transcript 24021. These are examples, Mr. Albiston. You've also said in your evidence that Mr. Cermak had an administrative function rather than an operative command. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, transcript 23766 to 7. That Mr. Cermak was not within the policing hierarchy; is that a fair representative of --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that is my reading of the documents, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Examples, transcript 23786, transcript 23825. And you've also addressed that officials of the MUP did not believe that Mr. Cermak had authority. Transcript 23807, transcript 23808. And you've referred to a relationship of cooperation, not subordination, in terms of Mr. Cermak's role with the civilian police. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Transcript page 23923, as an example to assist the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, just so that it's clear, Mr. Albiston, I am interested in whether or not Mr. Cermak -- at this stage in our questioning and answering during this part of the evidence, I'm interested in whether or not Mr. Cermak had de facto command and control over the civilian police. All right? Now, again, it's not in dispute, and if it is my learned friend will indicate so, that in your review of between 2.000 to 4.000 documents, and in the writing of your report, and in the selection of documents you looked at, is it right that the document collections included, for example, internal MUP communications between Moric and the police administrations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Documents between police administrations and police stations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Internal police administration memoranda?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Internal police station memoranda and notes of meetings between the military police and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Documentation between the military police and the MUP concerning coordination of activities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And documents relating to, for example, the staffing of police and the sending of separate police units?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Documents relating to passes, freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Some articles from the local press?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Criminal reports addressed to the higher echelons within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Documents which you say show Mr. Cermak passed on information to the police about crimes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Communications with members of the international community that Mr. Cermak had?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Documents within the international community network sent between their various bodies?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And minutes of meetings that were held with the international community, between them and Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, when you were considering these different collections, did you consider these collections in terms of de facto, or de jure, or both?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you were asked in detail about several of Mr. Cermak's orders to the police. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it right that you have reviewed all seven of Cermak's orders to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, it was put to you that they spanned between August to October, and I want us to look a little bit more closely at them, please, as a collection in the round.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, to assist the Bench, I'm going to call them up one by one relatively speedily, but I would ask, just to assist Mr. Albiston, if I could hand him a hard copy collection of the orders that I'm going to refer to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if Madam Usher could assist me by calling up P512, please, onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And for the record, as it's coming up, Mr. Albiston, you have it in front of you. It's an order dated the 8th of August, and it concerns UNCRO helicopters and their inspection. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it was addressed to the military police and the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Next document, please, P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just spent attention -- we paid attention to the P502.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was misinformed. I apologise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document on the screen, please, P53, which you have, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: An order addressed to the MUP and the military police, dated the 8th of August. And you will recall that it refers there to all UNCRO elements with clearly-displayed insignia may move freely in the areas of Knin and Drnis?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You see that one?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document, please, is under seal, so if it could not be put on the public screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You have it in front of you. It's D501, and I'll simply refer to it being of the date of the 10th of August, and the fact that it went to -- it's CC'd, it states, to the commander of the MUP and the headquarters, Administration of the MOHV. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Another August order, which is D303, 9th of August: "Immediately set up a team, members of military police and personnel from the Knin Police Administration with the task of finding the UNCRO vehicles." A document very familiar to you, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sent to the commander of the Knin police station and the commander of the Knin -- commander of the Knin police station and the commander of the Knin military police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going through these rather speedily, but the next document, please, is D503, 12th of August, and a similar sort of order here. Again: "Immediately form teams consisting members of the MUP ..." Again, teams from the MUP and teams from the military police with the task of finding and returning the stolen UNCRO vehicles?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The sixth order, which is still dated the -- in August, which is the 15th of August, P509?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, sent to the Knin police station and Knin military police, referring to the unhindered entry into the town of Knin at all check-points of the military and civilian police. Again, an order familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We have it on our screens there. I know the Bench is familiar with it. The seventh order is the only one, in fact, which is not in August, and it's dated the 11th of October, and it concerns there the temporary transfer of a part of MUP officers within the Knin police station to the old grammar school, sent to the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, my question in respect of these orders is the following: In terms of the seven orders, looking at the documents in the round, in your opinion, do they or do they not show de facto command and control by Cermak over the civilian police? And if you could give your reasons in your answer, Mr. Albiston, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the short answer is, No, and the reasons are as follows: If General Cermak had any genuine de facto command over the police in this area over this period of time, a period when certainly for part of the time, as we have discussed this morning, there were significant policing problems, I would expect to see a significant volume of orders, instructions, requirements for reports as to what exactly was being done about it. And I was questioned yesterday as to whether I examined both de facto and de jure concepts in my report. I think my report addresses the concept of de facto authority, but it was suggested to me that I had failed to address the possibility that General Cermak had or may have had some additional authority outside the legalistic approach, which it was suggested that I took to his authority; namely, some personal authority which had been granted to him by President Tudjman. And, of course, I have given some thought to this concept, and I think it's right that I should say to this Chamber that in all the documents that I saw, I do not see any evidence that this transaction whereby General Cermak was granted this additional authority outside the rules and regulations which I addressed, other than the suggestion which Ms. Gustafson put to me which arises from a meeting sometime later between President Tudjman and Mr. Cermak, and one other document which I think might conceivably be prayed in aid of that document, and I'm not sure of its number, but I'm sure that the OTP or the Cermak Defence team may be able to lay hands on very quickly, but there is a document in which President Tudjman says, and I think it may be he's addressing the press or more likely a private meeting, but he says words to the effect that either Brigadier Forand, by name, or the Canadians have some problems in South Sector, but I've sent Ivan Cermak, or General Cermak, who is a serious man, and these problems will be addressed. Now, in all the documents that I have seen, and I am quite certain that it well exceeds 2.000, I have seen no other indication of any informal or ultra vires authority over anything being granted to General Cermak. And if that authority had been granted, I cannot conceive how the police would have been expected to recognise and implement that authority unless someone had told them about it. And there is no indication that I've seen that anyone did tell them about it. Now, I have served in different police organisations and worked with many different police officers, and none of us take authority unless we recognise it and we've been told about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just to go back -- I'm going to ask you some questions about that in a moment, leading on from what you've said, but can I just go back, for the moment, to the orders? What observations do you have on the number of orders Cermak gave to the civilian police and the nature of their subject matter in relation to the issue of de facto command and control, please, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some elements of the orders are matters which most police officers would consider to be administrative rather than operational, and I think I addressed this Chamber previously on what I saw the distinction as being. Some of them are clearly related to problems arising in relation to the international community or matters which need to be addressed in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the document you referred to, which was a transcript concerning Tudjman stating that he'd sent a serious man down there, which is a document you draw our attention to --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the only one I could think of which might -- which I've read that might give substance to this concept of some sort of informal authority or authority which falls outside the documents which I studied which relate to the legal position for controlling the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Albiston, nowhere -- you've read that document. Nowhere in that document does it state that Tudjman gave authority to Mr. Cermak over the civilian police, does it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it certainly doesn't, but it -- I quote that document because I was trying to think, in fairness, from the point of view of balance, had I seen anything which I might have thought would support the argument which was put to me, and that's the only one I could think of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure where the line of questioning is going. But if it is going where it appears to be going, in the direction of the assignment of tasks by President Tudjman to General Cermak, then I have objections and submissions I'd like to make in relation to that, and it would be best -- be done outside the presence of the witness, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, now there's a problem, Ms. Gustafson. You say if it goes in this and this direction --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then I would like to -- because I would then have to establish whether the line of Ms. Higgins would go in a certain direction. Would it be good that either you're convinced that that's the way it will go, then we'll ask Mr. Albiston to leave the courtroom; if not, please verify with Ms. Higgins in which direction her line of questioning will further continue? Which of the two would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would prefer it would be verified with Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Why not you verify it? Why should this Chamber -- you apparently have an idea of what line of questioning would cause you some problems. Why would -- why not verify that with Ms. Higgins?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just don't think it's appropriate to direct [sic] her directly across the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- I'm happy to wait until she asks more questions and then I can object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you would not, microphone switched on, start a conversation with Ms. Higgins. At the same time, I do not see any problem in, microphone switched off, that you verify with Ms. Higgins, whether you could expect a problem to arise or not. But if you would prefer to wait and see in which direction it goes, then we'll invite Ms. Higgins to proceed. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to some questions in a moment concerning the topic that we've just been discussing, but I now would like to move into private session, please, to raise another matter with you, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm now dealing with the issue of freedom of movement, Mr. Albiston, so you know where I'm going. At some point yesterday, you were asked the question: "How did you come to the conclusion that it was Mr. Moric rather than General Cermak who was the man responsible for freedom of movement, in light of the fact that each of them had issued an order in this respect?" Do you recall that series of questions?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in your answer, you referred to the 3rd of August document from Josko Moric --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- which is, I don't think there's any dispute about, P493, as you referred to Tolj and Rebic --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- and that document refers to an order, in fact, by Josko Moric stating that journalists, foreign statesmen and so on can enter the liberated the territory at the said check-points in the operations area only by producing a passed signed jointly by Tolj and Rebic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to just ask you to take a look at D1769, please, and ask you whether this would assist you or not in answering more comprehensively the question you were asked about Moric or Cermak in respect to freedom of movement and why you said it was Mr. Moric. The first page here in front of us, dated the 8th of August, refers to the arrival of reporters and public figures in the liberated area. It was a document that I referred you to during my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If we can just go over the page, please. It refers to: "... without necessary permissions in the area of Petrinja and the Plitvice lakes, but permission from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the MUP is needed for other liberated areas." And if you refer paragraph 2 as well, towards the end, please. Now, does this document provide you with any assistance, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the assistant minister in the interior issuing a direct instruction on the 8th of August. It does mention, actually, in the second paragraph, Operation Povratak, the return operation, and I think there are other documents in the case which show that Mr. Moric, in particular, was concerned with this operation, and there would be implications for freedom of movement and authority to move in the area in relation to the management of Operation Povratak. So I think that would be an indicator, perhaps, of Mr. Moric's authority in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one last area that I wish to deal with with you. It was put to you yesterday that there was no evidence that anyone in the MUP thought that Mr. Cermak didn't have authority to issue P509, which was the order. You have it there in front of you in the orders collection. It was the order, if you recall, of the 15th of August, where the writing states: "From the 15th of August onwards, allow civilians unhindered entry into the town of Knin at all check-points of the military and civilian police on all axis roads to the town."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: What I'm interested in -- I'm grateful. Bearing in mind the question that you were asked by Ms. Gustafson --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- what I'm interested in and what we have looked at is the documentary background to this order, and I'd like us to look very briefly at the chain of documents in the series looking at the issue of whether or not anyone in the MUP thought that Mr. Cermak didn't have authority. I'm going to pull them up quickly onto the screen, the documents which you're familiar with, and ask you whether or not they assist you in answering that question more fully in the round.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, the first document, please, is D1014.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As it's coming onto the screen, you will recall this document. It's a document from Ivo Cipci, dated the 8th of August, and it refers to there being great pressure to visit the liberated territories. It's addressed to the Povratak section of the Ministry of the Interior, and the text refers to him asking to be provided with precise instructions as well as your opinion on the aforementioned problem, i.e., who to give passes to. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document is D494, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, again, as it's coming up, a document from Ivo Cipci, dated the 15th of August. And you'll recall, Mr. Albiston, this is a document whereby Ivo Cipci submits to the Povratak staff a copy of the pass for entering the garrison issued by Cermak, and it states: "Please reply and confirm the validity of the passes for civilian persons in question." You recall that document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you've seen there the writing at the bottom that we looked at in detail in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: "Cermak will issue an order on the annulment of travel passes? And freedom of movement"?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D495, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Again, this was the pass that was submitted with the writing at the bottom, which you've looked at before, handwritten. It states: "According to the MUP staff announcement, it is valid only for military personnel and civilians working in the Croatian Army. I will inform the staff of the MUP that all passes be revoked until further notice," et cetera. And that document should be just coming on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And just before we come on to P509, could I have D496 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: A document dated the 15th of August. Ivo Cipci again: "Please give us urgent directions as to how we should act." And the handwritten part, which you've looked at, in the top right section of the document, which states: "Call the Split-Dalmatia PU and say that Cermak will annul the passes today."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The next document, then, is P509, please, which is the order from Ivan Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And this was a document collection you looked at in that order, Mr. Albiston, in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have the paper copy here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, do these documents which I've shown to you assist you in answering the question more fully as to whether or not anyone within the MUP was challenging Mr. Cermak's authority?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just the question that Ms. Higgins was seeking clarification from cross-examination was whether anyone in the MUP thought that General Cermak didn't have the authority to issue P509 at the time. I'd just like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Albiston could bear that question in mind as well and answer in the round, I'd be grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the question of which I have just been reminded by Ms. Gustafson, I think the original answer I gave was, No, and I think that answer makes sense. This is a permissory dictum, if I can put it that way. To address Ms. Higgins' question about "in the round," I think the answer in relation to what the MUP at the time thought about Mr. Cermak's authority iis that so far as the MUP chain of command was concerned, going down to Mr. Cipci and looking at these documents, they did not believe that General Cermak was playing a role in Operation Povratak insofar as it related to the issue of passes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I'm grateful. I have no further questions for you. And I'm grateful to the Bench for the indulgence of an extra ten minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. I think it would be best, unless you'd finish within ten minutes, Mr. Kehoe, that we first have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do appreciate it. I will finish quickly. However, I think, in the interests of speed, I have a document that I'm not sure if the witness has seen or not seen. It is on the 65 ter list. It is an 18-page document. I'm not going to go through the whole document, Mr. President, but it may be easier, when the questioning begins, if the witness has the opportunity to take a look at this 65 ter document. It is 65 ter 2561. I did not consult with my colleagues yet on this score, but if, with their indulgence, they think this is a proper way, I would appreciate it. And, again, I think we might be able to move more quickly in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objections to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then we'll first have a break, Mr. Albiston, not until I've given Mr. Kuzmanovic an opportunity to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I similarly would -- it would be more expeditious. I have a document, which is a Defence exhibit, D692. It would make my cross-examination probably even much shorter if Mr. Albiston would have a chance to review that document. It's very -- it's not very long, Your Honour. It's a quick read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Albiston, you've informed us about the number of documents you've looked at. From now on -- you said 2.000 to 3.000, or 2.000 to 4.000. It will now be 2.001 to 4.001, or even 2.002 to 4.002. You'll be provided with the documents. We'll take a break, and we'll ask you to work during that break and read those documents. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to -- well, to further examine Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, you'll now be further examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just a couple of issues. The first issue I would like to clarify is a series of questions that you were asked by Ms. Gustafson yesterday, and this would be at page 24.033, line 25, going on to 24.034. And I read those numbers out for the purposes of the Chamber and parties, Mr. Albiston, but I'll read you the question and answer. "Q. So when you said, 'An examination of the documents in the case reveals that responsibility for the prevention of crime lay with the MUP,' would it be better to clarify that to be civilian crime?" And your answer is: "Yes, the investigation of crime, until such time as it is demonstrated that, in fact, it doesn't involve elements over which the civilian police can exercise that authority." If I could just clarify that a bit and put it in practical terms. The MUP has primary responsibility for crime until it is demonstrated that, for instance, a member of the HV was involved, and once it is demonstrated that a member of the HV is involved, primacy then turns to the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the next issue I would like to address with you is -- and these are meshed to some degree, but it has to do with the burial procedures, the pathological examinations, the autopsy examinations, that you referred to in the round with Ms. Gustafson. And did you have a chance to take a look at that document that I referred you to, that 18-page document, 65 ter 2561?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need to bring that up, but we're going to get to that, so -- it's an 18-page document, and I'm sure you understand why it was beneficial to take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you seen that document before today, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked a series of questions by Ms. Gustafson, and why don't I just go through these very quickly, your response. And if we could break it up a little bit, and please break-in at any point if I'm either moving too fast or -- which I tend to do, or you want to explain something. And this -- I would like to begin this questioning and your answers at 24.040, beginning at line 22. And Ms. Gustafson asked: "Now, on the issue of the procedure to be undertaken with dead bodies, you are aware, are you not, based on the evidence that you have reviewed, that a procedure was implemented after Operation Storm whereby dead bodies were treated as if they were combat victims, no on-site investigations were carried out in most cases, and the corpses were collected, identified where possible, and buried without conducting an investigation to determine the cause of death; is that right? Did you learn that? "A. It seems clear to me, from the documents, that that happened on a significant number of occasions, yes." Just turning -- Ms. Gustafson further clarified that, and we're going to break that question up a little bit, Mr. Albiston, when we get to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But if I can refer the Chamber and my colleagues to 24 -- excuse me, 24.043 at line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Q. And would you agree now that not investigating killing victims is a defect in that system?" Answer at line 13: "Well, as I stated in evidence, in ideal circumstances every death which does not have a certificate and an explanation should be treated by the police as a suspicious death and investigated accordingly, until such time it is found to be otherwise. I am not sure that was entirely practical in these circumstances, but I do accept your suggestion that there were bodies buried in circumstances which I, as a police officer, would wish had not happened, because I think even bodies with some element of decomposition may yield information to investigators." Now, if I can go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were reading, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sitting here in the back row, out of practice, so my apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, let me take this one by one and go into the alleged procedure that was presented by the Office of the Prosecutor on the examination of bodies. And if I can have you look at D235. Now, Mr. Albiston, well, the other document that I gave you was much more lengthy. This is only a two-page document. Again, I'm not sure if you've seen this before, dated 7 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the first full paragraph after the agenda and the numbers, it notes that: "Since in the area of army activity war operations are being conducted, it is crucial to carry out clearing up the terrain in that area, and it is our task to carry out the identification of persons in the prescribed manner, and it is not necessary to conduct on-site investigations." Now, you know, based on your examination of the documents, Mr. Albiston, that this was a decision that was made virtually on the heels of Operation Storm, where there was concern about bodies on the terrain, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And obviously it was August, which adds to decomposition and also adds to possibilities of disease, et cetera, prior to bodies being properly buried?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I may have misspoke with regard to the date, itself. This on the 7th of August, when military operations are still ongoing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you described, during the course of your testimony with my colleague, Ms. Higgins, and with my colleague, Ms. Gustafson, about a period of chaos and disarray which ofttimes is present both during combat operations and after combat operations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this policy that Ms. Gustafson refers to on page 24.040, about not examining dead bodies that were found, that was not a continuous policy of the Croatian authorities as we moved through August of 1995, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us bring up on the screen a document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 65 ter 2561, a Prosecution document. If we could bring that up on the screen. And, Mr. President, this document, and I say this for the clarification of the witness, itself [sic], we are -- from time to time, as we take them off e-court, there are documents with highlighting on these documents, and I do believe that as we see from the document on the screen, not so much on page 1, but certainly it begins on page 2, there is highlighting, and I just want to tell the Court we did not put that -- I certainly did not put that on there. It was just on there when I took it out of e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Albiston, you can see some faded highlighting in the document that you have.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, I read this document during the break. I didn't pay any attention to which areas were highlighted and which were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Now, just looking through this document, this is -- tell us about this document, Mr. Albiston. I mean, what did you see in this document, what did you conclude from this document about the procedures that were employed in this document, which is a 31 August 1995 report concerning the discovery of dead bodies in the territory liberated during Operation Storm in the Sibenik Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing I can say is that I have not seen this document previously. From a professional police point of view, it's quite an impressive document. I would say it increases my professional esteem for those who were conducting the operations which are described in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could just look at a couple of items, and certainly I don't intend to go through 18 pages of this document with you, Mr. Albiston. But in the preamble paragraph, it -- in the first page, this document is being sent, as you can see, by the crime police, and I think you can see it on the upper right-hand corner in the stamp that it's being sent to the District Public Prosecutor's Office in Sibenik. I don't know if that's abundantly clear, but you see the stamp in the upper right-hand corner. There it is, there it is, that stamp. It's being sent by the crime police to the District Public Prosecutor's Office, and this, we see in the preamble paragraph, it talks about these are bodies discovered during Operation Storm in both Sector North and Sector South.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the next -- if we can turn to the next page, again in the preamble paragraph -- in the first paragraph, excuse me, they are bringing to the pathology wards both civilians and combat casualties, are they not, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 7 of the document -- excuse me, page 6. Apologies. Now, these are bodies just globally found between -- the document reflects between the 4th of August and, I believe, the last one is -- in this report, in any event, is the 19th of August of 1995. And just if we go through the 16 and 17, we highlight civilians, or they're certainly identified of a civilian age, and they come from Kistanje. Do you see that? They're taken from the pathology department in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to the next page, and I'm interested in entry 22. Now, this is a report of 8 August 1995 involving a member of the ARSK named Nikola Vranjkovic. Now, it notes that he was wounded, and I'm talking about the last paragraph in 22, he was wounded by several projectiles fired during the night of 5 and 6 August, 1995, while combat actions in the Skradinsko Zaledje - pardon my pronunciation - were ongoing. He was transferred to the hospital by HV members in an ambulance on 6 August 1995. An external examination of the body and the autopsy were performed by Dr. Boris Brkic. If we can turn to the top of the next page, and this is the question I want to ask you about, the top of the next page, Mr. Albiston: "We have already informed the Military Public Prosecutor's Office of this incident in a special report," it gives the number, "dated 10 August 1995."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, that indicates quite clearly from the document that these entities of the crime police are conducting these autopsies and providing information to the appropriate authorities as they see it, be it the public prosecutor, which is a civilian arm, or the military prosecutor, which is a military arm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly the inference I would take from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your assessment of that as a professional police officer of many years' experience, how do you conclude? Is that a proper way to go, proper thing to do under the circumstances, as we find ourselves post-Operation Storm, August 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I think in combat, it's physically impossible to treat all casualties of combat as potential crime scenes or anything of the sort, but this document, which as I said earlier I haven't seen before, strikes me, in view of the dates to which it relates, as being quite impressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you did note in this document of other instances where information was passed on to the Military Public Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I read the whole document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me address with you, if I may, your comment about the practicalities. And I'm referring to what -- the quote that I had before of you saying regarding the burial of these bodies was not entirely practical under the circumstances, and I want to address that issue with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But before I do, I would like to offer into evidence 65 ter 2561.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D01783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just show you a -- several documents which are similar to some of the documents you saw before, especially the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could bring up on the screen D806. And, Mr. President, just by way of clarification, I use this document -- and if we could have the English translation. I believe it is the -- my colleague, Ms. Higgins, introduced a similar map with basically similar lines under 65 ter 2D00789. I was looking in e-court. I didn't see an admission on that. I may be mistaken, but as I was pulling it up from the records, was it just given an MFI number of 1778 or -- but this document, itself, was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 2D00789 was given Exhibit D01778, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll use this document, Judge, but therein was my confusion. And I can just use this for the purposes of this examination. The point will be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have to check why it was marked for identification. I don't remember, but perhaps you could assist us, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I do. I gave the Prosecution an opportunity to check the contents of the map, and I understand Ms. Gustafson said she had no problem with it. So, of course, that can be on the record and the exhibit number corrected in due course from MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the status of this document could already be changed now into an exhibit. That is, it is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for the record, I should clearly state that D1788 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think -- is it 1788 or 17 -- excuse me, I'm sorry, 1788. My apologies. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, this is a map quite similar to what you looked at, and what we have on the left-hand side is the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, with the green line in the middle being the liberated territory post-Operation Storm. And I believe, from the maps you had before, that virtually within 24 hours, the Zadar-Knin Police Administration Crime Police Section had another almost 6.000 kilometres to -- square kilometres to take care of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think on one of the maps I saw the figure was a little over 5.000 square kilometres, but I wouldn't quibble about the exact magnitude. Very large, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, sorry to interrupt you again. Where I sought to avoid confusion, I may have created confusion, because we now have D1778 and D1788, and I picked the wrong one to be admitted into evidence. It is D1778 which is now admitted into evidence. There was some confusion on the record. I interrupt you because otherwise if it comes a few pages further down, then people might be misled by that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about some of the practical circumstances here and highlight those. The Trial Chamber had the testimony of the public prosecutor, Mr. Galovic, who told us at page 19.677, line 5, to 19.678, line 4, that there were three investigative judges for the Zadar-Knin Police Administration prior to Operation Storm and after Operation Storm. Mr. Kardum, who you've referred to previously on occasion, noted for us that, and this is at page 9.325 to 9.326, line 6, that -- I'll just read the question to you. Question on page 9.326: "Q. Mr. Kardum, I think it's abundantly clear now on the record, but just to be certain, you had only 12 crime scene examiners subordinated to you during August of 1995; correct? And if you could answer yes or no, that would be very helpful. "A. That is correct." On the prior page, this is 9.325, line 16, at line 16: "The 12 crime scene examiners that I had in my police force prior to the Oluja were taken over -- they took over -- in addition to the regular duties which they normally did, they also took over assignments in the POW holding centre and partly also supported the sanitation effort." Now, as we go through the clearing up of these bodies, as an expert, consider for us and discuss with us, Mr. Albiston, the fact that the same three investigative judges now had well in excess of 5.000 square kilometres to take care of. I think you talked about the geographical distances. And then you had the same 12 crime police investigators who had that same area, while also having to deal with prisoners of war and other matters. I mean, what is the practical effect and the strain on a police department to have to cover that type of area while also crossing their T's and dotting their I's with you, if you will, with every body that may be found in August of 1995? Could you tell us and help us with that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the level of work generated, the distances to be travelled, the potential difficulties which would be involved in routing day-to-day travel at this period, and the numbers of persons involved measures against the numbers of jobs which they were being asked to do, is, by itself, a problem, and I think it doesn't need me to make a professional judgement or a guess. I think it comes through the documents that these people were extremely busy. And I think it may be worth remembering that when we're talking about crime scene examination, it's something rather more than going and taking photographs of a physical place or a body in a place. If we take, for example, the case of a suspected unlawful killing, the scene of the death will be a crime scene. The body of the victim will be a crime scene and will continue to be a crime scene as it is in transit. And when it is in the hospital or the -- whatever other place a post-mortem examination is carried out, the suspect or suspects will themselves be crime scenes that need to have forensic examination. And if the police officers and the forensic investigators are not very careful about how they behave, they will, themselves, become potentially crime scenes. So it's a very elaborate and difficult procedure, and it requires sufficient resources to address the numbers of cases which it's being asked to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we talk about this in very practical terms, using the map that's on the screen, hypothetically we have a body in Korenica in the north, a body in Donji Lapac -- the "D. Lapac" is Donji Lapac, a body in Kijevo, a body in Kistanje, assume that the sanitation teams found these bodies in these various locations, and you have three investigative judges with 12 crime scene -- excuse me, 12 members of the crime police who have all these other duties, what, as a practical matter under these conditions are the sanitation teams supposed to do under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're asking your senior officers to exercise good qualities of leadership and to establish priorities. And I notice, from the document which you showed me, Mr. Kehoe, that one of the questions which is addressed in the official form for setting out the response to this, it comes towards the back of the document which you gave me, gives an opportunity to explain why an investigating judge was or was not present at the scene of an on-site investigation, and, you know, the judge was not available or could not attend is one of the explanations as to why the on-site investigation can be carried on in his or her absence. I imagine that in these circumstances, that might be invoked from time to time. If you're discussing all the different areas in which the bodies can be found in the month of August in Croatia, then these people would have been very busy and, I hope, moving very quickly from place to place, but it would still have been a big task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not presenting to you, Mr. Albiston, that the police did everything -- crossed all their T's and did everything -- crossed all their T's and dotted all their I's perfectly in this. I'm not presenting that to you. But I submit to you, is it practical, in this situation, with all of the problems that you raise, command and control, communications, chaos, getting control of the area, was it practical to conduct a crime scene investigation for every body that a sanitation team found with only three investigative judges and twelve members of the crime police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my judgement, no, that wouldn't be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, thank you very much. I have no further questions. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
