utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe, as far as this document is concerned, which the witness read during the break, we see that there are brief descriptions of situations where bodies were brought to a place where they were examined. Is there any underlying material available?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will look. We took this from the Prosecutor's 65 ter list. I will consult with my colleagues across the well to see if there's additional documentation. I know that Mr. Misetic was scouring through our database yesterday to see if we could find additional documents. We did not find any. That being said, I'm not saying that they're not there, but we will take -- make additional efforts to find supporting documentation for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be further examined, Mr. Albiston, by Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Albiston.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 55 of your report describes your experience in Kosovo as United Nations police commissioner from 2001 to 2002 --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: -- where you were responsible for the command and control of 4500 police officers and the development of a multi-ethnic police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you had obviously, then, some experience in formation of a police force and the implementation or the attempts to continue the implementation of law and order in a post-conflict area; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The -- you had mentioned during the course of your cross-examination and re-examination by Ms. Higgins the Operation Povratak; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with what Operation Povratak is, are you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, insofar as it relates to the documents which I've seen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Operation Povratak was the Croatian Ministry of Interior's attempt to set forth and establish law and order on the newly liberated territories; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And is there anything that you saw about Operation Povratak which would lead you to believe that there was any flaw or anything wrong, obviously other than the limitation in resources, in its implementation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Limitation of resources, that's a matter for a government. That is -- that is the only way that I could see that improvements could have been achieved through -- from civilian policing perspective.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could we slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It's been a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So in essence, Operation Povratak, from your review of the documents that you saw, represented to you, at least, a legitimate attempt by the Croatian government to restore or create a situation in which there could be law and order in the post-conflict situation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly insofar as it relates to civilian policing and the establishment of civilian law and order, the documents which I saw indicate that there was a thorough attempt to achieve that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, over the break you had a chance -- or we gave you the opportunity to review what has been marked and previously admitted into evidence D692. Did you have a chance to review that, Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you had a chance or were you familiar with the contents of D692 before looking at it today?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I actually -- well, I certainly didn't read it as a Chamber document for this Chamber. I may have read it in my previous work. I'm certainly familiar with the subject matter which it deals with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the benefit of the Chamber and the record, this is a December 1999 report prepared by Mr. Bernard Kouchner, relating to the situation of the attempts to restore law and order to Kosovo prior to your coming there in 2001; correct.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 6 of that report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if we could pull that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph that starts, "We are deeply concerned ..." The paragraph begins: "We are deeply concerned about the situation of minorities. A close look at the trend in crime shows a clear improvement. A drop from 50 murders during each of the first weeks to 3 murders last week cannot be ignored." Now, at the particular time that this report was written, Mr. Albiston, the -- Kosovo was essentially being administered or policed by an international police force; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So during the time of an international police force's activities inside Kosovo, at least at some point there were 50 murders a week that had eventually dropped to 3?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you had a chance to review a great deal of documentation, and obviously you were not in Sector South or in the liberated territories immediately after Operation Storm, but at least from the documents was it your observation that the situation had improved after the restoration of the civilian police authorities or the implementation of Operation Povratak within the former Sector South, there was an improvement in the situation in terms of the nature and extent of the killings and crimes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Insofar --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Improvement from what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a confusing question, and I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I think you probably understood the gist of my question, but I'll try to make it a little less confusing. It's obvious that -- or you can tell me. Did you detect an improvement in the situation, the crime police, the level of crime, the amount of crime that went on within Sector South, after Operation Povratak? Was there an improvement, or did the amount of crime increase, did it decrease? Can you tell me that, from your review of the documents?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that the situation during the period which I reviewed improved. And if you're drawing my attention to comparisons with Kosovo, I think it would be fair to say that it improved more quickly in the area which this Chamber is considering than it did in the area for which I had responsibility subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you explain that briefly?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The killings, despite the presence of a significant KFOR military operation and a gradually increasing civilian police operation, continued in Kosovo for some time after what might be considered the watershed of June 1999. The nature of the killings changed, the nature of the criminality changed, and there was a steady reduction, but the difficulties, in my assessment, persisted longer than the difficulties in the area which the Chamber is considering after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, if we look at page 6 again, toward the bottom of this document, if we could -- the last paragraph, please. The first sentence, and this is referring to Kosovo, it says: "It took 15 years in Lebanon to achieve reconciliation. It cannot be done here," meaning Kosovo, "in six months." After your experience in Kosovo, and having dealt with implementing a policing system, and being responsible for the operational control and command of police officers, can you compare and contrast the situation relating to reconciliation in Kosovo to the situation in Sector South, if you can do so with respect to the documents that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm in a position to comment on community relations in the Sector South area on the basis of the documents that I have seen. My knowledge of that would be very scant by comparison to my knowledge of the other theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough. The last question I'd like to ask you -- actually, the second-last question relates to the last page of this particular report. Under "Conclusions" -- we'll wait for it to come up on the screen. Before we get to that, you had seen -- you had been to the area of Sector South; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes. I was there during April for a few days, April 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Kehoe had showed you on the map, I think it was D806 and there's no need for us to call it up right now, but the extent to which the increase in size had happened for the Zadar-Knin Police Administration; correct? You had seen that on the map?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I've seen the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And one of the factors, in terms of policing and investigations and processing of crime, has to do with the nature of the terrain, does it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to experience that terrain, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber, as -- I assume you'd never been there before.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd been in Croatia before, but I'd never been to the Knin area before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber the nature and extent of the terrain and what difficulties it would present from a policing standpoint?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly. The terrain is mountainous. The quality of the roads, when I visited them, was not good, and I have no reason to suppose that the quality of the roads was any better 13 years previously, certainly at the end of a military campaign, in view of the use of mines, shells, and the presence of heavy armoured vehicles and so on. It's unlikely, in my view, to have been better. So movement by road would be comparatively slow, and I think I've alluded earlier in my evidence to what problems that might generate. It also is not just a question of how quickly you get to a scene because of what we talked about in relation to crime scenes, suspects, witnesses, and so on, but it also inhibits the amount of work that you can get done during the working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, I'll go back to the conclusion in this document, D692. The last -- the first paragraph of the conclusion states, and this is in December of 1999: "It is clear that the deficiency in the law enforcement capability provided by the international community and the lack of sufficient assistance in the administration of justice has fostered the climate within which human rights violations documented in this report have taken place. Impunity for the acts committed has resulted from failures to conduct serious investigations, and this impunity, in turn, has perpetuated the violence." Now, I wanted to ask you, specifically, in that paragraph, in relation to your experience in Kosovo and trying to relate that experience to what you've reviewed for your expert testimony in this case. It's true, is it not, that at the time this report was written, and you've testified that it was the international community that was, for lack of a better term, responsible for the policing at that time --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it certainly was, yes. It's provided by the United Nations resolution. It's set out in 1244 of 99 that the responsibility for the administration of the province of Kosovo fell to the United Nations, and responsibility for policing it fell to civilian police provided by contributing countries of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it's true, is it not, that in your experience, at least in your review of the documents, that once the territory in Croatia was expanded for the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, there were many, if not the majority of those officers, that were not familiar with the new expanded territory, and the roads, and the places, and the -- where the events occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, there is evidence which I reviewed which shows precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the same situation that you had in Kosovo, people who were not familiar with the roads, were not familiar with the places, you had that same situation there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, we were all -- we were all foreigners, yes. Well, all the internationals, obviously, were foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I don't have any further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, you read, during the break, this report, and you said you were -- let me find it. I think you said you were impressed. Let me find your words exactly. Apparently, you did not use that word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said, Mr. President, it increased my esteem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professional esteem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll find you. Yes. You said: "From a professional police point of view, it's quite an impressive document." So "impressive" was on my mind. And you said: "I would say it increases my professional esteem for those who were conducting the operations which are described in the document."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw the document only after the break for the first time. Could you further explain what increased your esteem? From what I see in this report, that it's mainly bodies brought in for an autopsy were identified, and we find some description of what most likely and sometimes expressly is considered to be the cause of death. I do not see much police work in that, apart from autopsies and trying to find out or establishing what the identity of that person is. Could you explain to me what the -- how impressive this document is without knowing what other police activities have taken place?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this document was new to me. It shows police work being carried out or work which will assist police investigations being carried out in many cases on dates which are relatively early during the period which we're considering. It was, as I said, one that I haven't seen before, and it's reassuring to know that these basic procedures are being -- not only being carried out, but being documented here. There's a case in which a wounded man is taken away, who subsequently dies, but he appears to receive correct treatment. There are other examples of where the police are trying to describe what the circumstances of the death are, and this seems to me to indicate, in some cases at quite an early stage, attempts to run normal policing, and that is despite the difficulties of achieving that which I suggested in my evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in many of the reported cases, we do not find that much detail which you would wish to know about the circumstances under which that person died; seeing elderly people being brought in, 75, 80 years, bullet wound, that's it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. President, I don't know from this document whether what we are reading is intended to be a full forensic report on each individual case. I read it as a summary of a number of cases, I think 19 in number or is it -- maybe it goes up to 26, but, anyway, a good number of cases, and that this document doesn't purport to be a detailed rehearsal of all the evidence in every case. But maybe I'm wrong. It's the first time I've seen it, and I don't know what background material there may be which enables the author of this document to submit it for information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So would you then agree with me that without knowing why the forensic pathologist comes to the conclusion that someone was killed -- committed suicide by hand-grenade, what would have been the reason to believe that it was not someone else throwing a hand-grenade rather than --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the person who is, well, considered to have committed suicide, would you agree with me that without knowing the background, that it's rather difficult to give a fair assessment of how sound the police work was and perhaps follow up on what was reported.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would certainly like more information to give a better judgement, but I wouldn't necessarily expect to find that information in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you say it's quite an impressive document, and you say: "I would say it increases my professional esteem for those who were conducting the operations."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question that came to my mind is: I'd like to know more before I could assess the quality of the police work either prior to bringing in the bodies or as a follow-up of what apparently is established, including elderly people being apparently killed by shot wounds. Would you agree with me that for a good assessment, that you'd wish to know more?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I would like more information, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not an answer to my question. We all always want to have more information. Of course, I asked you whether --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for a sound assessment of the quality of the police work, whether you would need such information.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the distinction. I am impressed that this document exists at all in the circumstances in which we are describing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you explain why that surprises you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why it impresses you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we discussed yesterday, when Ms. Gustafson was asking the questions, about the quantity and the quality of investigations, and I agreed with Ms. Gustafson that, in my view, some of the achievements of the police -- the civilian police left something to be desired, this document seems to me to -- as the balance goes, it sits on the side of the balance which gives credit to the police, rather than the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- I do understand that. That's your appreciation of this document. I have no further questions. Ms. Gustafson, you are last in line.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Then, Mr. Albiston, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Albiston out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the -- yes, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. It's just one administrative matter which I'd like to clear up in respect of Mr. Albiston's testimony and a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour referred yesterday to D505, and we were looking at, firstly, the first letter of that document, and we undertook that we would upload a corrected version. The Croatian version, as you will remember, said the 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We have had the document checked, and it will be uploaded today, the English version, so that's corrected. The second-page letter that went with that document, we found is already, in fact, D1041 and bears the correct date in both versions, and again those documents have been checked, if that assists the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much for that. I nevertheless suggest that we keep the whole of the second page together with the other documents. It's -- unless all of it is already under that other number available. These were two documents, two different dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So D1041, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: D1041, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that -- apart from that, it bears the correct date, is it also the two-document exhibit or is it just the second one?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just the second letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the second letter. Then I suggest that for D505, that the correct version of the first page, that is, with the right date on it, as you said was uploaded, and then for the second document, that we have the correct version, as you say, as we find it already in D1041, it will be uploaded again --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- will be uploaded as well in D505, so that at least we have proper translations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have -- at one point we have a double, but I think it's better to leave it that way rather than to change it and to create a puzzle for those who are perhaps at a later time reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is the Cermak Defence -- I see, Mr. Cayley, you have changed positions. Is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. If I could just raise briefly two housekeeping matters. One is relatively straightforward. This witness has to return to the United Kingdom this weekend, I told the Trial Chamber, and I just wanted to respectfully remind you. It's Remembrance Sunday this weekend, and he has to leave sharp at 13.45. He will return on Sunday night to be with the Court again on Monday. And he simply asked me to respectfully ask you that. The second matter is, and I've spoken to Mr. Hedaraly about this, the witness produced a corrigendum this week in respect of the report that was filed by us in September, and he incorporated the corrections that he made into a version of the report. We would like to exhibit that version as opposed to the first version because, in essence, it incorporates the corrections. I've told Mr. Hedaraly that the witness has told me that the only corrections within the new version are those that are referred to in the corrigendum. It may be that Mr. Hedaraly wants some time to check that. And if so, it can be marked for identification and then admitted when the Prosecution is content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I think we have started checking, and I don't think there will be a problem, if that's the witness's representation. We'll just make sure that those are the only changes. But I have no objection, in principle, to the corrected report replacing the report that is now on file, to the extent that the changes will not result in substantial changes to the -- to also where the -- where the sentences are in the report for the sake of referencing. And I understand that the right pages now have been -- there was some issue with the wrong pages in the corrigendum, but I understand from Mr. Cayley that that has been fixed, so we should not have any problems with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the revised version, if that's uploaded, then we'll have that marked for identification until Mr. Hedaraly has finished his part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom. I do understand that it's Mr. Deverell. Meanwhile, I do understand that the parties were provided with the new court schedule for early next week, in which more detailed times are given, and that the commitment by the parties, that the evidence of Mr. Deverell will be concluded by Wednesday, is on the basis of this new scheduling scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Deverell. Mr. Deverell, before I'll invite you to make the solemn declaration, I'd like to explain to you that I commonly address witnesses by "Mr.," and that's not in any way to be understood as disrespectful for rank, academic qualifications, et cetera. It's just the way in which we address witnesses, the Bench does, address witnesses who are supposed to give their evidence or their expert evidence, as all other witnesses. Mr. Deverell, Madam Usher will now hand out to you the text of a solemn declaration, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deverell. Please be seated. Mr. Deverell, you'll first be examined by Mr. Cayley, who, as I take it you know, is counsel for Mr. Cermak. And in order to avoid whatever nervosity, this Chamber will adjourn at a quarter to 2:00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just for purposes of the record and before we begin, General Deverell, I have told you this before, but just to remind you, between us our interpreters, who are translating into the French and Bosnian-Croatian-Serbian language, so it's helpful, one, if we both try and speak slowly, but steadily, and, secondly, if you take a break between my question and your answer, and that way they'll keep up with us. Just for the purposes of the record, your name is General Sir Jack Deverell, and you are a retired British Army general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we can have in front of you 2D00790, which is your updated report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you incorporated, within this version of the report, the matters you identified in your corrigendum this week?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this the report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Your Honours, that could be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D01784, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the next document, if we could have 2D00791, and if the witness could be shown the second page and the third page. And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this the corrigendum that you produced for your report this week?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And they are largely corrections to footnotes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And there are some textual changes in there, too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if I could apply for that to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Maybe I got confused, but if the new report incorporates all of these changes, I thought that was the reason why we would admit the new report -- or discuss the new report into evidence, to obviate the need to have a report and a corrigendum into evidence. So if we have the new report which incorporates the corrigendum corrections, I just don't see the purpose in having the corrigendum into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the purpose of the corrigendum, Your Honour, is to identify the changes that the witness has actually made. It's in the interests of transparency so that everybody knows what has happened, so I would like it to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, no objections, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D01785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that document can already be admitted. It doesn't -- there's not a need to be MFI'd first. Therefore, it is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the last document is 2D00792.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Deverell, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It is an additional note which discusses my involvement with the Cermak Defence team, and also covers some of my other commitments that I have been involved in during my time whilst I'd been involved in this particular trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is this an accurate reflection of all of the contact that you've had with the Cermak Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it's not, because I'm afraid, by my own stupidity and inefficiency, I failed to translate from my notes onto the -- onto the actual document one other visit, which I would like to ask the Chamber to allow me to insert, and that is between the 21st and 25th of April, 2008, I visited The Hague and attended some court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, this now on the record, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Perfect, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I don't think that we need a new additional note to be drafted. May I take it that you want to tender this additional note?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would like to tender that document, yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D01786.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could just briefly look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a fairly self-explanatory document. What I'd like to briefly ask you about are the issues related to the original report that you filed and the work that you were requested to do on the report after that initial presentation to the team. Could you explain exactly what you did?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked, because it was felt that the report was too long and contained too much repetition and, therefore, was not as focussed as it -- as it should have been, and I was very happy to accept and agree to that criticism, and therefore I did change the sequence of the report, and I also, as a result, managed to, I hope, remove some of the unnecessary repetition, although some is still there. And that was really -- that was really it. It was a removal of repetition and a change in the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you specifically refer, in your note, to the discussion about Grubori. What were you asked to do there?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I was asked to remove what you could call my -- my précis of what happened at Grubori, my workings, almost, which was, Mr. Kay said, would be dealt with elsewhere. I was happy to do that. It didn't change my conclusions about Grubori, which remain in the report, and neither did it -- clearly did it change my view of that particular incident. And I was -- I was willing to conform with that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you state, at the end of that particular section on that page, that the team made it clear from the outset that it was your report and that you had a duty to ensure that the views represented were yours and yours alone. I'm putting it in the sense of referring to you. Can you just expand on that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I was constantly righted by the team that it was my duty to reflect my views in my report, and I had no difficulty with that. Quite obviously, I knew that was to be my -- that was my duty. But the team were -- took great pains to make sure that whatever -- whatever discussions that we had, whatever things might have been mentioned, that I had to be -- it had to be my view and I had to be confident that it was entirely my view and it had not been influenced by them. And as I said, at the end, and it is quite clear, and I mean what I've said, this I have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And lastly in this document, on the last page, if we could have the last page, in terms of your other professional obligations, I don't want to go through them with you, but is that an accurate representation of the other activities that you'd been involved in?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes. There's the odd smaller thing I'm involved in, but it's insignificant and doesn't influence what I've done in this -- this particular part of my -- my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the first part of your report -- do you have your report to hand?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you also have, I think, the bundle next to you of the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what I'm going to do, in order to try and accelerate the process, is to show you documents on the screen, as opposed to having you try to go through that bundle of footnotes and trying to find the documents, which I think is going to take a lot of time. If you could turn, please, to part 1 of your report, these are your biographical details. I do not intend to go through all of the details of a long and distinguished career. I simply would like to ask you some questions that are relevant to this particular evidence that you're giving here today. Is it right that you've commanded at every level in the British Army, up to and including a brigade?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it's right to say that between 1997 and 2001, you were the deputy commander of the UK Field Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how many men were within the UK Field Army at that time? And women, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Approximately 75.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Between 2001 and 2004, what position did you occupy?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I was Commander-in-Chief, Allied Forces, Northern Region, which is a NATO appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And can you very briefly tell the Court what that particular position involved?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I was a subordinate commander to the supreme allied commander, Europe, an American full general. There were two subordinate commands, Allied Forces North and Allied Forces South, and I was responsible for the northern half, which is essentially from the Alps to the North Cape. It was a command which had no soldiers. Those soldier-sailors and airmen would have been assigned to us in the event of a conflict, in the event of the security of Northern Europe being -- being affected, and it would have been in the probably hundreds of thousands, the low hundreds of thousands, as a force. And I was responsible for three subregional headquarters, Norway, Denmark and Germany, and two what were called component headquarters, a maritime headquarters in the United Kingdom and an air headquarters in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And during that period of time, I think you were the operational commander of the first NATO force in Afghanistan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you commanded that operation from Brunssum, in the Netherlands, from your headquarters in Brunssum --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I did. There was a lieutenant general in Kabul who was conducting the day-to-day operations. I gave him what was termed operational direction from Brunssum, where my headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to go back in time a little bit to talk about operations in which you'd been involved, I think, as a young infantry lieutenant, you served in Aden in 1966. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And can you just briefly tell the Court what you were doing there?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Aden was an area of South Yemen, at the end of the Arabian Peninsula, and we were involved in counter-insurgency operations against a political -- a series of political militias who were trying to ensure that the British left the British colony of Aden, and it was essentially internal security. It was low-level violence from militias involving small arms, grenades, et cetera, and more serious violence in the rural areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From 1969 to 1986, I think you spent a total of six years in Northern Ireland. Again, very briefly, can you tell the Court what you were doing and the positions that you occupied?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I started off in Northern Ireland commanding a platoon of about 30 men, and I finished in 1986 commanding a battalion of some 600 men. The situation in Northern Ireland was extremely confused, especially in the early days, and it was an internal security issue. There had been a breakdown of law and order. There was an attempt to change the political structure through violence, and there was a religious -- a religious interface problem as well. That developed and changed throughout the time. And in the border areas there was a different form of violence. It was not public violence, it was not public disorder, but it was attacks on security forces, police and soldiers, and also civilians from different religious and political groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What experience have you had of dealing with the United Nations during your career?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I was once, for four months, the commander of a company of about 120 men who had a role on the Green Line in Cyprus, wearing Blue Berets, as part of the United Nations operation to monitor the cease-fire arrangements between the Turks and the Greeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What experience in the former Yugoslavia do you have, if any?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Between September and the end of February/beginning of March 1998-1999, I was the deputy commander operations, so I was responsible for directing the operations of the NATO sustainment force based in Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our job was to ensure, in particular, that the two-entity armed forces obeyed the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now let's move into the meat of your report. I'd like to move around, so I'm not going to be going in any order and I will not be asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I'm looking at the clock. Since you are changing subjects, I wonder whether this would be a good time to have a break so that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, I think it's a very good time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 1:00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General Deverell, one last question based on the prior subject that slipped my mind. Have you had experience, as a senior officer, in dealing with international organisations such as the UN, the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have, mostly in -- almost entirely in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when we had a United Nations high representative out there, and I dealt particularly with the United Nations High Commission for Refugees and the International Red Cross and a plethora of other organisations. And, of course, I also had some dealings when, in particular, setting up the operation in Afghanistan, in Kabul.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dealing with the same issue, the interface between military forces and the international community?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move, as I said before, into the main part of your report, and if you could turn to part 4. And here you address general principles of command and control and subordination in the armed forces. Are principles of command and control and subordination fairly common across all military forces or are they not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: In my experience, they're common across all military forces in, you know, developed countries, with armed forces that look very similar for clear reasons; that armed forces tend to do a similar job, whichever country they belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you refer in your report to something called military doctrine. Can you explain very briefly to the Judges what you mean by "military doctrine"?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, it's the over-arching philosophy which -- from which everything else flows, your structures, the way you approach things, your equipment, the numbers of soldiers you have, the balance between your navy, army, and air force. In some countries, doctrine can be rather prescriptive. It can tell people what to do. In other countries, Britain, for example, doctrine is very much about telling you how to approach matters, how to think, how to deal with a complex problem, in terms of how you approach it, which then leads you to take decisions as to what you will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what you understand "command and control" to mean?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It used to be just "command," but -- deemed as just "command," but really since the Second World War the word "command and control" has come in. The "command" is this sort of -- how can I describe it? It's the conceptual activity, it's the analysis of a problem, and it is the way a commander and his staff use their intellect and judgement and experience to come up with solutions to complex problems. The "control" element is the mechanistic element. It's, of course, radios, it's telephones, it's satellites, it's computer capability, but it is also process and procedure, how many meetings you have, who is in those meetings, what those meetings deal with. It deals with something we call battle rhythm; that is, the way the staff actually support the commander in his analysis, his decision-making, his planning, and in the implementation of that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Going to part 4(e) of your report, where you address the issue of unity of command and subordination, what do you understand by the meaning of "unity of command"?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Well, it is -- it's fundamental. One of the principles of military effectiveness is actually unity of purpose. When you consider that war is -- conflict is the breakdown of normal processes, the breakdown of society, if that's the way you wish to define it, then the military have to find sort of coherent ways of dealing with that, and therefore it is very important you have this unity of purpose. And you can only -- as far as I'm concerned, you can only achieve that if you have one person responsible for a task, whether that task is a big task or a small task, and that one person has to have the unity of command. He has to know who he is commanding, and those who are commanded by that person must understand that they are commanded by that person. And it is all about tasking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say "it's all about tasking," can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes. A military mission is -- is divided into specific tasks, and people are allocated tasks, and they are obliged to carry out those tasks. That is the reason they are in command, whether that is command of a large organisation or the command of a platoon or a section of seven or eight men. And it is very important that that task is clearly defined. It is sometimes limited in time and space and duration, and, of course, the essential element of the task is that the person has the resources which enable him to do it, or her to do it. So there is a very strong resource implication there which the commander, the senior commander, has to take into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Talking now specifically about subordination, what do you understand "subordination" to mean?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: "Subordination" is quite simply the authority given to somebody to task a person or a group of people, a group of units, in their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you find that the principles of unity of command and subordination were reflected in Croatian Army doctrine?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: They're laid down absolutely clearly. It's one of the -- one of the guiding principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, please, we could have P1116 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1186"] on the screen, and it's Article 49 of that document. I believe it's on page 21 of e-court. That may not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just while we're waiting, General, for the purposes of your report, did you review both JNA and Croatian Army doctrine from the documents that you were provided with?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you'll look at the English version on the left-hand side, and if you look at Article 49 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Perhaps the screen, Madam Registrar, could be adjusted so that the witness can see the entire English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but I read on the transcript it says "P1186." It's the right document on the screen, but just for later on, so that there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. It's P1116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've covered much of this in what you've already said, but now looking at it in the perspective of Croatian Army doctrine, do you have any comments on Article 49?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I can only see half of it still, but I think I can see the most important bit. It says clearly that it shall be based on -- sorry, can you make it smaller? Thank you. I can see that, thank you very much. Thank you. It says really what I've just commented, that it's based on the basic principles of unity of command and the obligation to carry out decisions, commands, and orders of a superior. And I would find that written in different ways in all sorts of documents in guiding military forces in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it refers to one superior. What is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That there is one person who must be responsible for a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move on, and I'm afraid we're going to have to go backwards a little bit in your report to part 3, where you deal with the normal training and background of general officers. Now, you retired from the British Army as a full general, I think what is sometimes known as a four-star general in NATO terminology. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And what I would like to know is the training and experience, very briefly. And I know that we dealt with your career. I don't need to repeat your career details, but the training and experience that you had throughout your career in order to rise to the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't quite -- I didn't quite catch that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you is this: Obviously, you've referred to your biographical --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- details. I don't need to go through that again, but what I'd like you to outline to the Judges is the training and --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- experience that you've had throughout your career to get from the lowest which you were in the army to a full general.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's essentially three levels of military training, and again these tend to be common throughout certainly Europe and the United States and other similar areas. The first is the basic level, the foundation training, which is teaching young officers, men and women, how to command their soldiers at the tactical level, and it introduces them to military law, administration, logistics, welfare. It provides the foundation knowledge they need. Depending how successful they are in that, you then get, after about ten years, to a third level -- I'm sorry, a second level, which is really preparing you for more important posts up to and including lieutenant colonel, perhaps working in a superior headquarters or a Ministry of Defence, and you start then getting into the implementation of higher-level policy and, of course, command at a higher level. And then for a relatively few number of officers, there is a third level which -- for which you can be selected, and that takes you into the political-military interface. It prepares you for senior command appointments, two-, three, or four-star, to use the NATO terminology. You will be trained amongst civilians -- with civilians and civil servants, sometimes the police, and it is focussing you -- focussing on trying to train you in order to create policy rather than merely implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many years' training have you been through during your entire career, do you think?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I would suggest that probably I've probably done something like six years' full-time training on courses over four months in duration in my 40-odd years, including initial officer training.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please have D1007 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying, General, while we're waiting for that to come on the screen, that you were provided with some information, with information that the Cermak Defence team had on Mr. Cermak's background, were you not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a decree, first of all, posting Mr. Cermak to be a reserve officer of the Croatian Armed Forces. And if we could scroll down, I think there is a second document within that, and this is a decree on appointment. Do you -- can you see that clearly?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I can, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you've seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the rank of colonel general, does that rank exist in the British Army?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Not by that name. It's the equivalent, I believe, of lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to the first document. Do you refer to this document in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the particular part that I'd like to know if you know anything about is where it says: "To the rank of colonel general, administrative service." Does that phrase mean anything to you, "administrative service"?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Not specifically, but it says -- what it says to me, clearly, is that General Cermak's future employment should be limited to administration of some sort within -- within an administrative area, no doubt because of his previous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the study that you made of Mr. Cermak's background, can you make any comment to the Court on how qualified you felt he was for the position of colonel general in the Croatian Armed Forces? As a military man, I'm speaking here specifically.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Well, from the evidence I saw, from the documents I read, I found no evidence that he had ever been in the army in a meaningful way; that he'd been a general because he was the assistant chief of logistics, because that is what the Croatian government did, and that he had had none of the experience that I would have thought would have been required for somebody to be given the sort of -- or to be given an active role in the Croatian military. I think I say in my report he was uniquely unqualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, uniquely unqualified for what?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: For a military role.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can we now please look at part 6 of your report. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And this is addressing the subjects of garrisons, generally, Knin Garrison and the Croatian Army garrison commander. General, have you ever been a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I have. Between 1988 and 1991, when I was commanding a brigade, I was also the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to the Court what a garrison commander is?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I say in my report garrisons to armies are to armies what ports are to navies, and that is true. They are the sort of -- the static base from which operational units are deployed to train or to conduct operations, wherever those operations might be. They're the place where the families, if there are families, live and are looked after. They're the place where they leave their equipment behind to be looked after which they're not taking on operations. There are a mass of other issues which are required, and other resources and capabilities which are required to maintain those units, to give them the support they require, both administrative and training support, whilst they are there or whilst they are deployed elsewhere. They are the essential underpinning of your military effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are they peacetime or wartime structures?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: They are, in my experience, peacetime structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, have you looked at Croatian Army doctrine on garrisons?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please have Exhibit D32, and this will be page 11. I'm told by my case manager it's page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And is it referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It is referred to in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, first of all, in terms of comparing the garrisons that you're familiar with to the garrisons at least you saw from the regulations in Croatia, are they similar or dissimilar?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: No, I think that that represents what I would have expected to see, in general terms, in dealing with other garrisons, and British garrisons, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, looking at Article 52: "The garrison commander is responsible for placement, order, discipline, and service in the garrison." Now, I want to essentially break this sentence down and then go to the next sentence. What do you understand by the meaning of the word "placement"?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That is a word, I believe, which is used to mean billeting or accommodation, and we would have used the word "accommodation."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Accommodation for what?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: For soldiers, and their families, no doubt, but essentially for soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And then dealing with "order, discipline -- order, discipline ... in the garrison," what do you understand that to mean in terms of the garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: "Order" I take it to mean -- and to a degree it's linked to service. "Order" is all about providing the services required in the garrison, those support services. For example, it might be eating arrangements. It might be refurbishment capabilities, the repair of vehicles. And the "order" bit is that those capabilities -- those resources are properly managed, that they are opened at times when it is convenient to those that are you supporting, the units, to make use of them, and that they are properly organised, that they're properly sustained, and that the units, themselves, know that perhaps their slot is between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning and another unit goes there between 10.00 and 11.00, so you don't get overcrowding. That is the meaning, in my mind, of "order." It is the good ordering of the resources and the people who work for the garrison commander who are responsible for running those resources -- those capabilities. "Discipline" is what underpins it. It is the capacity of a commander to impose those rules on people and have the ability to sanction them if they break those rules. "Service," as I've said, is linked with "order," and I think in this instance it means that the garrison is supposed to provide a 24-hour service; for example, a duty officer who can be used to deal with whatever incidents might occur during your 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've stated in your answer that essentially these terms apply to eating arrangements, refurbishment capabilities, repair of vehicles. What kinds of facilities are these?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: They're largely static facilities, and they're logistic support facilities or administrative facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the next sentence, which states: "All units and institutions within the garrison are subordinate to the garrison commander in matters of order, discipline and service." Can you explain to the Court what you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I understand that to mean that the unit commander -- I'm sorry, the garrison commander can expect units making use of those facilities to obey his instructions, the instructions of the garrison. For example, and I've used this example before, that is, timings of the opening of the dining hall, the allocation of timings for units to use refurbishment facilities, or laundries, or any of those other support -- support elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does it -- does this provision apply simply to units moving through the geographical area of a garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Because that would immediately interfere with the unity of command, if the garrison commander could task or impose tasks upon a unit which was not subordinated to him just because it happened to be in the garrison area. What is expected, as a unit moves through a garrison area, is that it obeys, for example, speed limits imposed by the garrison or route directions put in place by the garrison, and that is an expectation which is well known. It is accepted as part of the way you do your business. It doesn't have to be laid down. It is an expectation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, without going through them in detail, if you look at Article 54, and specifically 54(c), do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that the kind of activities that you would expect a garrison to be involved in?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does that bear any similarities to British garrisons, those particular activities?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It's similar. I've never known a British garrison to be responsible for bathing in rivers, lakes, or the sea, but the rest -- the rest is pretty accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could now please look at D34. And just one moment. It's page 2, Madam Registrar. Actually, if the witness, I'm sorry, could just be shown the front page so that he can confirm that he's seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And is it referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It is referred to in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page, and if we could please look at paragraph 2, have you considered that particular paragraph, General?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, what I'm particularly interested in is the phrase: "The garrison commands do not have an operational function or the right to command HV units, except precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order and discipline in the garrison," et cetera. I won't read the rest of it. Can you explain to the Court what you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and it goes back to what I said in my -- one of my previous answers, because it actually says that the garrison commander does not have an operational function or the right to command HV units, except when they are engaged in using the facilities of the garrison; that is, those facilities which we've previously seen, whether they be laundries, bathing in lakes, training facilities, ranges, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that what you would expect to find?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: That's what I would expect to find, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the next paragraph, which is paragraph 3, and I won't read it out, but you can see what it states. Can you explain to the Court what you understand the meaning of cooperation and coordination of tasks of the garrison with the bodies that are listed there? And if it assists, you can actually give examples from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, garrisons exist within the civil structure of a country. That's plainly obvious. And they rely -- almost certainly they will rely, and in my experience, which I will talk about in a second, you rely on the support of that civil structure, whether it be for your utilities, water, electricity, other fuel, whether it be for welfare services to help you deal with your families, employment services for the employment of families and relatives, and the police -- the civil police, for either national disaster, terrorist activity, or the fire service because you depend upon them for their support in fighting fires, there are a mass of structures out there which will support that garrison. The garrison does not have the capability to do it itself. That is exactly my experience when I was a garrison commander, and we regularly had to cooperate with the police and the -- those who gave us -- supplied us with our utilities, and to a degree coordinate our activities so that the garrison could be properly supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in terms of your interpretation of this provision that we're looking at here, can you say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the garrison commander was tasked here to establish levels of cooperation with other government departments in order that the garrison should be able to play its proper role both in the support of the armed forces and as part of, because it existed in, that civil structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when you were garrison commander, that relationship that you had with the police, did that put you in command of the local police?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: No, it did not. And if ever one gave the impression that you were about to tell the British police what you would wish them to do, you were reminded very firmly that you were not in charge of the police. They were very much -- they very much had primacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, let's look briefly, please, at D33. And this is, I believe, pages 9 and 10 -- I'm sorry, pages -- it's the last five pages of that document. If we could just -- this is D33, yes. If we could have, please, the last five pages of that document. The last four pages, I'm sorry. Yes, perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, again, General, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you refer to it in your report?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you explain what you understand this document to be?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: This is -- we would call it an establishment table, and it gives the total numbers and breaks down those numbers into separate component bits for any particular organisation, military establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you have them in the UK?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges, based on the actual establishment figures and the manning figures, and we know this is for the Knin Garrison on the 31st of August, can you describe to the Judges what type of headquarters this was?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It's a very small headquarters and will not have a great deal of capability. As we can see, it's only got five officers, three civilians, so -- and nine people, a total of nine people. It means it's a headquarters that is supporting a commander with very limited tasks and very limited authority and responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And how large would an operational headquarters be?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It depends exactly what the task of that headquarters is. But as a guide, you would find brigade headquarters in a developed -- developed -- the armed forces -- I'm sorry, the armed forces of a developed country would probably have something in the region of 40 to 50 officers responsible to support the commander, and they would be split up into -- into disciplines; administrative, logistic, planning, intelligence, communications, et cetera. And there's a whole raft of NATO doctrine which dictates that within a nation, and each one would have its own head and a certain number of officers, and, of course, soldiers to support those disciplines. And they are the people who provide the specialist advice to help the commander analyse, decide, plan, and implement, and then monitor the implementation of the plan. They are the people who do the coordination and help with the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just bearing in mind all of the documents that you -- that we've just addressed, the garrison regulations, the size of the headquarters, I want you to consider briefly the following. Now, you were provided, I believe, with a copy of the indictment in this case at the beginning of the case, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And did you read that document?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I just want to briefly put to you a narrative from that indictment, and I would like you to comment on it. And this is paragraph 7 in the last indictment, and it reads as follows: "In his combined capacities, Ivan Cermak participated in various structures of power and responsibility and possessed effective control over members of the HV units or elements who comprised or were attached to, or operated in the Knin Garrison, and also over civilian police who operated in the garrison area and areas adjacent to it. The HV units comprising or operating in the garrison and adjacent areas included, without limitation: The 4th and 7th HV Brigades; the 1st Croatian Guards Brigade (1 Hrvatski Gardijski Zdrug); the 113th Infantry Brigade; 142nd Infantry Brigade; 144th Infantry Brigade; 126th Home Guard Regiment" - I'm not going to try and pronounce that - "the 6th Home Guard Regiment; the 7th Home Guard Regiment; the 134th Home Guard Regiment; and a combined Military Police Company." Now, putting aside for one moment the military police, which we will come to later, can you give your comments on that narrative, please?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It struck me, when I saw that part of the indictment and I then looked at the size, experience, and skill sets, if I may use that jargon, of Knin Garrison in August of 1995, that it was my judgement that that headquarters was not in the position to exercise any form of control at all of those units that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier in your evidence, and you explained the meaning of the term -- that the garrison commander did not have operational control of HV units. Does that also affect your position in respect of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Well, of course, it is stated quite clearly in regulations that he did not. But even if he had done, by whatever means, and I saw no evidence of this at all, the size of his headquarters, the experience of the people in it, and his own experience would have made it, to me, extremely difficult, to the extent it was inconceivable that he could have exercised any form of control -- operational control over those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the documents that we provided to you, did you see any orders from Mr. Cermak to those units?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any reports from those units to Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does that have any significance for you?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: It does. I mean, you -- you can't -- you can't control tactical formations, as these were, which by definition are spread out on a battle-field which was very expansive, without issuing them with orders, and you cannot understand what they are doing. Therefore, you are incapable of analysing the situation, and, therefore, deciding and planning and then implementing a new plan, unless you receive reports which contain necessary and important information back from them. And I saw no evidence of either that information being sent by those units to Knin Garrison headquarters, for the attention of General Cermak, nor did I see any orders given by him to those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the provisions -- the narrative that I've read to you essentially suggests that Mr. Cermak possessed effective control because these units were -- who comprised or were attached to or operated in the Knin Garrison. Have you seen any evidence at all that these units were part of the Knin Garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I've seen no evidence that they were part of the Knin Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you seen any evidence they were attached to the Knin Garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
