utterances.text: I've seen no evidence that they were attached to the Knin Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in terms of operating within the garrison area, would that have subordinated them to the Knin Garrison?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: No, but it would -- because it would have been -- it would have undermined the whole concept of the unity of command and -- sorry, it would have undermined the whole concept of unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could move, please, to part 3(b) of your report. And you actually speak of this in a number of parts of your report, but I'm interested in lines 12 to 15 of your report on page 8, where you state that there were three elements to Mr. Cermak's appointment. And we've dealt with the first one already, that the garrison -- was Mr. Cermak a classical garrison commander, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: No, he certainly wasn't, on two counts. Firstly, he had none of the experience that you would have expected a garrison commander to have. And, secondly, he was a colonel general rather than a major or a colonel. Therefore, he was over-ranked, in my -- in my judgement, he was over-ranked for that particular role.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say that he had two other roles, and we'll go into these in more detail next week, but you say: "Secondly, he was an ad hoc administrator to facilitate the normalisation of Knin." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Well, he was sent by President Tudjman with a sort of - can I use the phrase - a general direction to sort out -- I think the phrase I heard was to sort out Knin, and I know we will be maybe discussing that in more detail later, but from my point of view, that meant that he was involved in the urban regeneration of Knin, getting the trains, the drains working, opening the shops, getting the banks working, getting civilians back, and starting -- starting the whole process of regenerating Knin as part of a civil society.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And have you seen evidence to that effect? We'll look at some of that --

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, lastly, this last position that you say, as appointed contact for international organisations, can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: His direction from the president, I think -- and this again was slightly vague, he said he was told to go and help the Canadians. He became, I believe, the point of contact really by default, particularly because he happened to be a very senior officer by rank. And my experience of international organisations, and having been part of one, myself, is that you do tend to look at -- to seek the most senior officer present and make a presumption -- an assumption that he has the power that you would normally associate with somebody of that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you actually experienced that, yourself?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I have. I fear that I've done it myself. It is partly -- it's part of the human dynamic, really. You're trying to get somebody who has the capacity to deliver and somebody who can deal with you, so that you can do your business as effectively and quickly as possible. And I think it's a natural instinct for those who are confronted with a very confusing and dynamic situation, members of the international community, to try and seek those they believe provide them with the capacity to deliver that which they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in terms of his position as garrison commander, these other two functions that you've identified, urban regeneration, you call it, point of contact, were they part of the job description of a garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And do you draw any conclusions from that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes. The appointment of garrison commander gave him none of the authority or responsibility that he -- or none of the authority that he required to do the other two jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could please now look at 2D00632.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, there are many documents in this case, and you've referred to this in a number of places in your report, but I'm not going to refer you to all of them, where you address the issue of military governor. Have you seen documents in the case where Mr. Cermak is referred to by members of the international community as the military governor?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, 2D00632.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think that's 65 ter 2D.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, did you, in fact, find for the Cermak Defence team a definition in your NATO -- I think it's US Department of Defence/NATO Dictionary of Military Terms?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page of that document. Just, Mr. President, for explanation, obviously we're not going to offer the entire dictionary into evidence. This is just an extract, and we've provided the parties with the web site so that people can inspect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a definition which you found, General Deverell. Can you explain to the Judges what you understand a military governor to be?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- the military governors appear to me, from this, to be a post and appointment that is only required when you are in a foreign country, a different country, and the civil structure has broken down, that the rule of law is no longer respected, and that you do not get the normal pegs of civilian -- of civilian authority in place, and by default, the army -- the military organisation is seen to be the only one which has the capacity to exercise control, in terms of rule of law, and perhaps to operate the utilities -- the basic utilities of life. And therefore a military governor can sometimes be appointed with a military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say "when you are in a foreign country." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Well, if you're operating outside your own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, specifically, it states in this definition "in an occupied territory"?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you give the Judges any examples that you know of where a military governor was appointed?

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: I believe I'm correct, in terms of Laws of Armed Combat, that all forces have a responsibility, as they take ground, to provide those essential support elements for the population that they liberate or otherwise. The evidence I will use or the example I will use --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, because I think maybe you didn't understand my question. I want you to give an example of a military governor.

utterances.speaker: JACK DEVERELL
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. The British military governor in Germany at the end of the Second World War is an example of the absence -- with the breakdown of Nazi Germany and the civil authority there, the vacuum was filled by military governments provided by both -- by France, the United States, Russia, and Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I'm looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and in view of the wish of the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether this --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's a good place, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deverell, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether testimony already given today or still to be given next week. And we'd like to see you back Monday morning, 9.00. We adjourn, and we resume on Monday, the 9th of November, at 9.00, Courtroom III.
